transfer.scenario: Re-use your design for an engineering assistant over released design specs, where only the latest released revision may be cited and export-controlled specs are restricted. What changes?
rubric: abstain rather than cite unreleased drafts

brief: A 4,000-person logistics company wants an internal assistant that answers employee questions about HR, IT, travel and safety policies. There are about 6,000 policy documents (PDF and wiki pages) across three regions. Some documents are restricted to managers or to HR. Policies are revised often, and last year a wrong leave answer from an outdated PDF caused a grievance. Leadership wants answers with sources, and wants the assistant to say when it doesn't know. The company already runs on AWS.

clarifications.reveal: Around 50 documents change each month. HR wants a change visible to the assistant within 24 hours of publishing.
Access is by groups in the corporate identity provider: all-staff, managers, HR, and region (US, EU, APAC). About 8% of documents are restricted.
PDFs live in a document management system that can export to S3 nightly; wiki pages have an API. Some PDFs are scans with tables.
Expect up to 1,500 questions a day, with peaks on Monday mornings. Target is an answer within 5 seconds for most questions.
Regions can have different rules for the same topic. Employees should get their own region's policy by default.
People will ask personal questions like 'how many leave days do I have left'. That data lives in the HR system, not in policy documents.

HR will provide 200 real past questions with correct answers. Leadership's bar: no restricted content shown to the wrong group, and wrong answers rarer than today's helpdesk error rate (not yet measured).

constraints: Restricted documents must never reach the model for users outside the permitted groups.
Policy changes must be reflected within 24 hours.
Every answer must cite the document, section and version it relied on.
When sources don't answer the question, the assistant must say so and route to the right helpdesk.
Personal data questions are out of scope for policy retrieval.
Company runs on AWS; managed services are preferred where they meet requirements.

acceptableArchitectures.name: Managed RAG with Bedrock Knowledge Bases
acceptableArchitectures.summary: Nightly S3 export and wiki connector feed a Bedrock Knowledge Base with a chosen embedding model and vector store; each document carries metadata (groups, region, version, effective date); syncs run on a schedule or on change events; the application calls Retrieve with metadata filters built from the user's authenticated groups and region, then generates with a grounded prompt and structured output (answer, citations, abstained). Optional Guardrails grounding check. AWS feature details are UNVERIFIED and must be checked.
strengths: Built-in chunking options, sync and citations
Faster to production for a small team
tradeoffs: Less control over parsing scanned PDFs and tables
Filter expressiveness and limits depend on the service and vector store
Must verify that sync timing meets the 24-hour requirement
Using Retrieve plus own generation adds code but gives control over prompt and abstention; RetrieveAndGenerate is simpler but less controllable

acceptableArchitectures.name: Custom pipeline with hybrid search
acceptableArchitectures.summary: Own ingestion jobs (parsing with OCR and table handling, structure-aware chunking with headings, version metadata) write to a search engine that supports BM25 and vectors (for example OpenSearch); queries run hybrid search with permission and region filters, then a reranker; generation through a model API with a grounded prompt, citations and abstention.
strengths: Full control of parsing, chunking and ranking
Hybrid search handles policy codes and form numbers
Easier to instrument each stage for evaluation
tradeoffs: Team must build and test sync, deletion and permission logic

acceptableArchitectures.name: Hybrid routing: RAG for policies plus system-of-record tools for personal data
acceptableArchitectures.summary: Either RAG design above for policy questions, plus a router that sends personal questions ('my leave balance') to an authenticated HR-system API call instead of retrieval. Introduces agent-style tool use, which is Module 2 material.
strengths: Answers personal questions exactly instead of guessing
Keeps personal data out of the document index
tradeoffs: Adds routing errors as a new failure mode
More scope than a first release may need

challenges.challenge: Why not fine-tune a model on all 6,000 policies?
expected: policies change monthly: retraining each time

challenges.challenge: Why not put the policies in the system prompt? Context windows are huge now.
expected: corpus too large for one call
restricted docs would be in every prompt

challenges.challenge: A manager in the EU gets a US policy answer. Where do you look?
How do you prove a non-HR user can't see salary bands?
A policy changed yesterday and the assistant still gives the old answer. What failed?
How do you know it's ready to launch?
expected: test set from 200 real questions plus unanswerable and restricted cases

mustCover: permission filtering at retrieval from authenticated identity
freshness mechanism meeting 24 hours, including deletion of superseded versions
separate retrieval and generation evaluation before launch
strongSignals: routes personal-data questions away from RAG
handles scanned PDFs and tables as a parsing risk
logs retrieved chunk IDs for debugging
names at least two architectures and their trade-offs
marks AWS specifics as to-be-verified rather than guessing
redFlags: access control only in the prompt
no plan for updates or deletions
evaluates only on a demo or end-to-end vibes
